div.p: Despite their industrial relevance, contemporary textbooks do not pay much attention to cyclic executives, if at all. Analysis techniques for these executives are therefore needed.

In this paper, we consider the impact of a real-time system model on the schedulability analysis of basic single-rate cyclic executives. Next to the basic real-time scheduling model M B , presented in [1], two other models are considered in this paper, a first refined model M R that takes the notion of observable event [2] into account and a second model M P that in addition also considers the single-path code paradigm [3]. Whereas the exact schedulability analysis for M B turns out to be pessimistic when applied for the refined model M R , the analysis turns out to be optimistic for the second model M P .
Index Terms-cyclic executive, real-time system model, schedulability analysis 2022 CPSSI 4th International Symposium on Real-Time and Embedded Systems and Technologies (RTEST) |

div.head: A. Background and motivation
div.p: The academic interest in cyclic executives has gradually decreased since it was concluded in the paper of C. Douglass Locke [4] that for hard real-time systems the fixed-priority approach generally dominates the cyclic executive approach. As a result, contemporary text books, such as [5]- [8], mention cyclic executives but hardly address them in detail. In a recent survey in the field of real-time embedded systems involving 120 industry practitioners [9], it was observed that the question which task scheduling policy/policies are used in the considered systems, 54.17% of the 97 respondents answered "static cycle/table driven/time-triggered", amongst other policies. Given their industrial relevance, proper explanation of cyclic executives and their analysis therefore remains desirable. Exact analysis for (basic) single-rate AFAP (as fast as possible) and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives for a basic real-time system model has been presented in [1]. In this paper, we present analysis for a refined model, in which the notion of observable event [2] is taken into account.

div.head: B. Problem description
div.p: Hard real-time systems require timely responses to events. These system responses shall be provided neither too late nor too early relative to the occurrence of an event. This is illustrated by, e.g. an air bag, with an inflation as a response to the occurrence of a collision (an event). The interval from the arrival of an event to a response may therefore be constrained by a system specification by both an upper bound, which is also called a worst-case system deadline, as well as a lower bound, which is also called a best-case system deadline. These deadlines for the system give rise to timing constraints on realtime tasks. When control is realized in software, such as in hard real-time computing systems, these tasks typically poll sensors (to detect events) periodically and use actuators (to provide responses).

In this paper, a hard real-time system is assumed with a set of n (input) events and a set of n (output) responses. Between events and responses, a 1-1 relationship is assumed. Events are sporadic, i.e. are characterized by a minimal interarrival time. A best-case and a worst-case system deadline is associated with each event-response tuple. The worst-case system deadline is assumed to be at most equal to the minimal inter-arrival time of the event. A dedicated real-time polling task handles a specific event-response tuple.

We assume a single-processor system and a basic singlerate cyclic executive. The cyclic executive executes a statically known sequence of tasks in a continuous loop. Every task occurs exactly once in the sequence. The 'classical software design' step of assuming fixed periods and deadlines for tasks, as is done in [10], is not needed for our approach. This makes the analytical approach presented in this paper inherently different from existing approaches in the literature. The problem addressed in this paper is how a system model M influences the schedulability of a system S under a basic single-rate cyclic executive C.

div.head: C. Contributions
div.p: In this paper, schedulability analysis for basic single-rate cyclic executives is presented for a refined real-time system model M R , in which the notion of observable event [2] is taken into account. We compare the results with the analysis for a basic real-time system model M B presented in [1]. We briefly consider the consequence of taking the single-path code [3] paradigm into account as well.

div.head: D. Organization
div.p: The organization of the remainder of this paper is as follows. In Section II, we recap a basic model M B and present a refined real-time system model M R . The basic single-rate cyclic executives are recapitulated in Section IV. Worst-case analysis of these cyclic executives for the refined model M R is the topic of Section V. A comparison of the cyclic executives for M R can be found in Section VI. A comparison of the schedulability analysis of cyclic executives for the basic and refined model is presented in Section VII. In Section VIII, we 978-1-6654-9910-1/22/$31.00 ©2022 IEEE briefly discuss the consequence of taking the single-path code paradigm into account. Section IX concludes the paper.

div.head: II. REAL-TIME SYSTEM MODELS
div.p: We start this section with recapitulating the basic model presented in [1]. We subsequently present our refined model.

div.head: A. A basic real-time system model M B
div.p: A system S, a set E S of n (input) events e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e n , a set R S of n (output) responses r 1 , r 2 , . . . , r n to these events, and a 1-1 relationship between events and responses is assumed. Events are sporadic, i.e. each e i ∈ E S has a minimal interarrival time WT S i . Each event-response tuple e i , r i has a bestcase system deadline BD S i and a worst-case system deadline WD S i , that shall satisfy 0 ≤ BD S i ≤ WD S i ≤ WT S i . In addition, a set T S of n independent, 'regularly' polling tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n is assumed. A task τ i polls for (i.e. senses) event e i and provides response r i . Each task τ i has a bestcase computation time BC i and a worst-case computation time WC i , that shall satisfy 0 < BC i ≤ WC i . The term job is used for the execution of a task. We denote a job of task τ i by ι i,k , with 0 ≤ k. The first job of τ i is therefore denoted by ι i,0 . For a job ι i,k of task τ i , its computation time C i,k shall be at least BC i and at most WC i , i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∧ 0≤k BC i ≤ C i,k ≤ WC i .
div.p: To denote the start time and the finalization time of job ι i,k , we use s i,k and f i,k , respectively.

Tasks are assumed to be executed on a single processor, are scheduled by a (basic) cyclic executive, run non-preemptively and do not suspend themselves. Moreover, we ignore scheduling overhead and system initialization.
We assume that the jobs of tasks in a cycle are executed in the order of increasing index for ease of presentation and without loss of generality, i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i<j≤n ∧ 0≤k s i,k < s j,k .

div.head: B. A refined real-time system model M R
div.p: The basic real-time systems model can be refined in two orthogonal directions. Firstly, the notion of observable event [2] 1 can be taken into account, i.e. the end of a task's execution need not coincide with the last observable event of a task (in our case a response). Secondly, given the 1-1 correspondence between events and responses, there will be no response when a job does not detect an event.
To address these two aspects, the model can be refined by distinguishing additional notions of best-case and worst-case computation times of a task τ i , e.g.
• BC r i and WC r i : the best-case and worst-case computation time for task τ i to provide a response, respectively;

• BC nr i and WC nr i : the best-case and worst-case computation time when no response is given (i.e. no event is detected) by τ i . 1 In [11], the notion of observable event is discussed in the context of fixedpriority preemptive scheduling.
For these additional notions, we assume2

div.head: III. PROBLEM FORMALIZATION
div.p: Timing constraints for 'regularly' polling tasks are derived from the system deadlines for the refined model M R in this section. Moreover, both best-case and worst-case schedulability conditions for the tasks as well as the system are presented. When a system S meets all its (worst-case and best-case) deadlines for a specific model M under a specific cyclic executive C, and a specific sequence of tasks task[], the system S is called schedulable for M, under that cyclic executive C and that sequence task[]. We briefly compare the schedulability conditions for M R with those for the basic model M B in [1]. This section is concluded with a problem formulation.

div.p: For a 'regularly' polling task τ i , a best-case situation arises when the event occurs immediately before a job ι i,k polls for the event and ι i,k requires its best-case computation time BC r i to provide a response; see Fig. 1. The following timing constraint for task τ i is therefore derived based on start times and response times

div.head: B. A worst-case schedulability condition for M R
div.p: The worst-case situation is more complex. On the one hand, we can exploit the fact that the introduction of the notion of observable event allows us to consider the response time r i,k , rather than the finalization time f i,k , of a job ι i,k of a task τ i when checking whether or not a system deadline WD S i is met. On the other hand, this also implies that whenever a next event arrives immediately after ι i,k provides its response, the next job ι i,k+1 may experience an additional delay of at most f i,kr i,k due to the execution of ι i,k .

We therefore have to consider more than just a single pair of jobs. For a 'regularly' polling task τ i , an initial worst-case situation arises when the job ι i,k polls for the event e i just before e i occurs and the next job ι i,k+1 detects and handles the event, i.e. provides a response; see Fig. 2. div.p: This condition is essentially a conjunction of a best-case and a worst-case schedulability condition. We can make the following three observations when comparing the schedulability conditions for M R and for M B . Firstly, the best-case schedulability condition (5) for M R is independent of a specific cyclic executive, like the bestcase schedulability condition in (8) for M B . Secondly, M R allows more systems to meet the best-case schedulability condition than M B , because of (1). Thirdly, the worst-case schedulability condition (7) for M R considers an extended worst-case situation, whereas the worst-case schedulability condition in (8) for M B only considers the initial situation. As a result, the worst-case schedulability condition (7) for M R looks considerably more complicated than the condition for M B . We take a closer look at the worst-case schedulability conditions of both models in a next section when presenting worst-case analysis of single-rate cyclic executives.

div.head: D. Problem formulation
div.p: In this section, it has been illustrated that the refined realtime system model M R allows more systems to meet the bestcase schedulability condition than the basic real-time system model M B . Exact best-case analysis of a system S is trivial (for both models) for (basic) cyclic executives scheduling nonpreemptive tasks. Focus in this paper is therefore on exact worst-case analysis for basic single-rate cyclic executives for the refined model M R and its comparison with the analysis for the basic model M B .

For the refined model M R , it has to be guaranteed that task τ i ∈ T S provides a timely response r i upon detection of an event e i , i.e. before the (worst-case) deadline WD S i of the system S. We therefore have to derive a test to check whether or not (7) holds.

div.head: IV. A RECAP OF BASIC SINGLE-RATE CYCLIC EXECUTIVES
div.p: Tasks can simply be implemented as procedures for (basic) cyclic executives, and executed within a loop. For a singlerate cyclic executive, every task is executed exactly once in a cycle. Two basic types of single-rate cyclic executives are recapitulated in the following subsections, AFAP and timedriven AFAP. serve that tasks are constantly being executed by the processor.

div.head: B. Single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive
div.p: For a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, a cycle is started by a timer. Because the (worst-case) executions of the tasks must 'fit' in a cycle, the sum of the worst-case computation times of all tasks shall be at most equal to the inter-arrival time T S of the timer, i.e. A single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive gives rise to spare time, i.e. a combination of slack time 3 and gain time 4 . This spare time can be used to run the processor at a lower, more energy efficient, clock frequency after the cycle is completed or to execute background tasks.

div.head: VI. A COMPARISON OF CYCLIC EXECUTIVES FOR M R
div.p: We compare the single-rate cyclic executives from a schedulability perspective for the refined model M R in this section. We merely observe that for other aspects, such as jitter, energy efficiency, and implementation overhead, we may draw similar conclusions for M R as for the basic model M B in [1].

div.head: VII. A COMPARISON OF ANALYSIS FOR M R AND M B
div.p: In this section, we prove that from a scheduling perspective, the refined model M R (strictly) dominates the basic model M B . Stated differently, whenever a system S meets all its deadlines under a basic single-rate cyclic executive C for model M B , it will also meet all its deadlines under C for M R , and there exist systems that are not schedulable under C for M B but are schedulable under C for M R .

div.p: Lemma 2. When a system S is schedulable under a singlerate AFAP cyclic executive for the basic model M B , it is also schedulable under that cyclic executive for the refined model M R .

Proof. From Section III-C, recall that when the best-case schedulability condition holds for a system S for the basic model M B , it also holds for refined model M R . The lemma is therefore proven when meeting worst-case deadlines of S under a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive for the basic model M B implies meeting these deadlines for the refined model M R . We prove the latter by showing that (17) in Theorem 4 implies (10) in Theorem 1. We address the two conjuncts in (10) separately. The first conjunct in (10) follows immediately from (17) by applying ( 2) and ( 4). The second conjunct is derived from (17) as follows
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n WC i + 1≤j≤n WC j ≤ WD S i ⇒ ∀ 1≤i≤n WD S i ≤ WT S i ∀ 1≤i≤n WC i + 1≤j≤n WC j ≤ WT S i ⇒ ∀ 1≤i≤n 1≤j≤n WC j ≤ WT S i ,
div.p: which proves the lemma.
Theorem 6. From a scheduling perspective, the refined model M R dominates the basic model M B for the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive.

Proof. Using Theorem 4, we derive that system S II can not be scheduled under a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive for the basic model M B . The result now follows immediately from Lemma 2 and the fact that for the refined model M R the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive can schedule system S II , whereas for the basic model M B it can not. Lemma 3. When a system S is schedulable under a singlerate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive for the basic model M B , it is also schedulable under that cyclic executive for the refined model M R .
Proof. Similar to the proof of Lemma 2, we use (4) to derive (13) in Theorem 2 from (18) in Theorem 5, which proofs the lemma.
Theorem 7. From a scheduling perspective, the refined model M R dominates the basic model M B for the single-rate timedriven AFAP cyclic executive.

Proof. Using Theorem 5, we derive that system S III can not be scheduled under a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive for the basic model M B , nor does it become schedulable when the order of the tasks are changed.

The result now follows immediately from Lemma 3 and the fact that for the refined model M R the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive can schedule system S III with the order of tasks changed, whereas for the basic model M B it can not.
Based on Theorems 6 and 7, we conclude that the exact schedulability analysis for the basic model M B may yield pessimistic results for the refined model M R .

div.head: VIII. DISCUSSION: SINGLE-PATH CODE PARADIGM
div.p: For the single-path code paradigm, a single execution trace is produced for programs [3]. Combined with instruction timings that are data-independent, the execution time of singlepath code becomes constant with respect to input data. On time-predictable hardware, the best-case and worst-case computation times of a task τ i are therefore the same, i.e. BC i = WC i . This paradigm yields another real-time system model M P , when taking the notion of observable event [2] into account. For the additional notions introduced in Section II-B, we now assume
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n BC r i ≤ WC r i ,
div.p: because the response may be provided at more than one (but still mutual exclusive) place(s) in the code. Moreover, similar to the refined model M R , a task may still perform some work after providing the response, i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n BC r i ≤ BC i , (19
div.p: and
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n WC r i ≤ WC i .
div.p: Finally, for BC nr i and WC nr i , i.e. the best-case and worst-case computation time of task τ i when no response is given, are identical to its best-case and worst-case computation times BC i and WC i ∀ 1≤i≤n
div.formula: BC i = BC nr i = WC nr i = WC i .
div.p: From these equations, (19) gives rise to an anomaly compared to the basic model M B , because the best-case schedulability condition ∀ 1≤i≤n BC i ≥ BD S i for M B for system S becomes optimistic for the model M P . Stated differently, a system S that is deemed schedulable based on the best-case schedulability condition for model M B , i.e. will meet all its bestcase deadlines, may miss a best-case deadline for the singlepath code paradigm. For model M P , the following best-case schedulability condition is therefore required
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n BC r i ≥ BD S i .
div.p: We leave further investigation of schedulability analysis for model M P as future work.

div.head: IX. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we considered the impact of a real-time system model on the schedulability analysis of a system S under two basic single-rate cyclic executives, AFAP and timedriven AFAP. We first considered a refinement of a basic real-time system model M B [1] that also takes the notion of observable event [2] into account. The best-case schedulability conditions for this refined model M R and the basic model M B turned out to be similar. The worst-case schedulability condition for M R turned out to be more complicated than the condition for M B , however, because multiple worst-case situations may have to be considered for M R . For the refined model M R , we derived exact best-case analysis for both basic cyclic executives, sufficient worst-case analysis for the AFAP cyclic executive and exact worst-case analysis for time-driven AFAP cyclic executive. Moreover, both cyclic executives were briefly compared from a schedulability perspective for M R . Finally, we proved that the exact analysis for M B may yield pessimistic results for M R .

We briefly considered a further extension of the model with the single-path code paradigm [3], a model which we baptized M P . It was shown that the exact best-case analysis for M B may yield optimistic results for M P . Based on these findings, we therefore conclude that the real-time system model has a significant influence on the schedulability analysis of systems for single-rate cyclic executives, and specifics of models shall therefore be carefully considered.
Topics of future work include exact worst-case analysis for the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive for M R and worst-case analysis for cyclic executives for M P .
